problem: Every action taken on a computer system — reading a file, running a script, connecting to a database, sending an email as the company — has to be attributed to someone or something. Without a concept of a "user," a system has no way to know who is asking, whether they're allowed, or who to hold accountable afterward.
Businesses run into very real trouble when user accounts aren't managed deliberately:
A former employee's account stays active for months after they leave, quietly retaining access to email, file shares, and internal tools.
Two people share one generic login ("support1") to save on licensing, and when something goes wrong, no one can determine who actually did it.
A new hire waits three days for a working account because provisioning is a manual, undocumented process, delaying their first day of productive work.
A service account created years ago for a one-off migration still has domain admin rights and nobody remembers why, becoming a standing security risk.
An auditor requests a list of every account with access to financial systems, and the answer takes a week to compile because accounts were never centrally tracked.
A user account is the fundamental unit of identity an operating system or directory service reasons about.
Everything this roadmap has covered so far about permissions is meaningless without a reliable, well- managed concept of "who" — this session is where "who" gets defined.
concept: A user account is a record the operating system (or a directory service like Active Directory) maintains to represent an identity — a specific person, or a specific automated process — that can authenticate and be granted rights on a system. Every user account has, at minimum, a unique identifier, credentials or a way to verify who's presenting the identity, and a set of associated attributes (home directory, shell, group memberships, expiration date).
Three broad categories of user accounts recur across every environment:
Interactive/human accounts — tied to a specific person, used to log in and do work.
Service accounts — used by an application, service, or scheduled task, never meant for interactive human login.
Built-in/system accounts — created automatically by the OS itself (root, Administrator, SYSTEM, daemon accounts) to run core OS functions.

A simple mental model: a user account is an employee badge. The badge itself doesn't grant access to any specific door — that's what permissions and group membership do (Session 20, and the next session on Groups) — but without a badge, the building's security system has no way to know who's even trying to get in.
deep: 3.1 Linux/Unix user accounts Every Linux user is represented internally by a numeric UID (User ID), not by their username — the username is just a human-friendly label mapped to that number. Core account data lives in /etc/passwd (one line per user: username, UID, GID, home directory, shell), while password hashes live separately in /etc/shadow, readable only by root, specifically so that ordinary users can't even attempt offline password cracking against it.

UID Range Typical Meaning 0 root — the Linux superuser, unrestricted by standard permission checks 1–999 (varies by distro) System/service accounts created by installed packages (e.g., www-data, mysql) 1000+ (varies by distro) Regular human/interactive user accounts Key account lifecycle commands: useradd/adduser (create), usermod (modify), userdel (remove), passwd (set/change password), chage (set password expiration policy).

3.2 Windows user accounts Every Windows account is uniquely identified by a SID (Security Identifier), a long structured string (e.g., S-1-5-21-...-1001) rather than just a username — this is why renaming a Windows account doesn't break its permissions, since the SID underneath never changes. Local accounts are managed via Local Users and Groups (lusrmgr.msc) or PowerShell (New-LocalUser), while domain accounts are created and managed centrally in Active Directory (Session 52) via Active Directory Users and Computers or PowerShell's ActiveDirectory module (New-ADUser).
Local accounts exist only on one machine and are meaningless anywhere else on the network.
Domain accounts are created once in AD and can authenticate against any domain-joined machine, which is the entire point of centralized identity at enterprise scale.

Built-in accounts like Administrator and Guest exist by default and are prime hardening targets — best practice is disabling or renaming the default Administrator account and enforcing use of named, individually accountable admin accounts instead.

3.3 The authentication vs. identity distinction A user account itself is just an identity record — it doesn't, by itself, prove that the person logging in actually is who they claim. That proof is authentication (passwords, MFA, Kerberos tickets — covered in a managed object; verifying the account holder is a later topic.

3.4 Account lifecycle states State Meaning Active Account can authenticate and use its assigned permissions normally Locked out Temporarily blocked, typically after repeated failed login attempts, as a brute-force defense Disabled Deliberately deactivated by an admin — the standard first step when someone leaves, preserving the account for audit history without allowing login Expired Passed a configured expiration date, common for contractor or temporary accounts
workflow: User account management is one of the most continuous, recurring operational workflows in any IT department:

Onboarding (provisioning): creating the account, setting an initial temporary password, assigning it to the correct groups (Session 22), and setting up mailbox/home directory — ideally via an automated, templated process rather than manual, inconsistent setup.
Access changes: updating group membership and attributes when someone changes role or department, rather than simply adding new access on top of old (which causes "permission creep").
Password resets: one of the highest-volume help desk ticket categories anywhere — exactly the kind of ticket a support/CEx role handles constantly.

Offboarding (deprovisioning): disabling the account immediately upon departure (same day, ideally same hour for involuntary terminations), removing group memberships, and only deleting the account later per data retention policy.
Periodic account audits: reviewing for stale, unused, or orphaned accounts — a classic finding in security audits is accounts belonging to people who left the company a year ago.
Service account governance: tracking what each service account is for, who owns it, and rotating its credentials on a schedule rather than leaving a password unchanged for years.
enterprise: User accounts sit directly beneath Permissions (Session 20, the previous topic) and Groups (Session 22, next) in Layer 2, and are the foundation everything in Layer 4 — Identity (Active Directory, LDAP, Kerberos, SSO, MFA) — is built on top of. A local Linux or Windows user account is the simplest form of this concept; Active Directory and LDAP scale the same idea to thousands of accounts across an entire enterprise.

In a Windows enterprise, domain user accounts created in Active Directory are what workstations, servers, email (Exchange/M365), VPN, and internal applications all authenticate against — a single well- managed AD account is often the one credential controlling access to dozens of downstream systems (this is exactly what SSO in Layer 4 formalizes). In Linux environments, user accounts might be purely local, synced from a central directory via SSSD/Winbind, or managed via configuration management (Ansible/Puppet) across a fleet of servers.
6. Dependencies (what Users rely on) Depends On Why Kernel (Session 12) The kernel maintains the actual UID/SID-to-process mapping and enforces which identity a running process is tied to.
File Systems (Session 19) User account data itself lives in files (/etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, Windows SAM database) that must be stored, protected, and backed up like any other critical data.
Permissions (Session 20) A user account is meaningless as an access concept without a permission system to check it against — the two topics are inseparable in practice.
Processes (Session 13) Every running process must be tied to a user identity; the OS cannot launch a process without resolving it to some account context, even a system one.
Boot Process (Session 8) System/service accounts (like SYSTEM on Windows or daemon accounts on Linux) are active from very early in boot, before any human logs in.

7. Dependents (what relies on Users) Depends on Users Why Groups (Session 22) A group is fundamentally a named collection of user accounts — groups have no meaning without underlying users to contain.
Active Directory (Session 52) AD's entire purpose is centrally hosting and managing user account objects at enterprise scale.
Kerberos / SSO / MFA (Sessions 54, 64, 65) All authentication mechanisms exist to verify that whoever is presenting a user account's credentials is actually that account's rightful owner.
Services (Session 17) Every Windows service and Linux daemon runs under a specific user account context, whether a dedicated service account or a built-in system account.

Logging / Auditing (Sessions 18, 82, 99) Meaningful audit trails depend entirely on actions being attributable to a specific, individually accountable user account rather than a shared or anonymous one.
Incident Response (Session 100) Investigating any incident starts with identifying which user account(s) were involved and what they had access to.
security: Individual accountability: shared/generic accounts ("admin", "support1") destroy the ability to attribute any action to a specific person — a foundational reason enterprise policy almost universally requires one account per human.

Prompt deprovisioning: the single highest-value, lowest-effort security control in this entire topic is disabling accounts the moment someone leaves — delayed offboarding is a consistently exploited gap in real breaches.

Standing privileged accounts: permanent admin/root-level accounts used for daily work create unnecessary risk; Just-In-Time (JIT) or Privileged Access Management (PAM) approaches grant elevated rights only for the duration needed.

Service account hygiene: service accounts often have powerful, broad access and rarely-rotated passwords, making them a favorite lateral-movement target once an attacker has any foothold — dedicated governance and credential rotation matter disproportionately here.
Default account hardening: renaming/disabling built-in accounts (Administrator, Guest, root remote login) removes low-effort, well-known attack targets.

Account lockout policy: automatically locking an account after repeated failed login attempts defends against brute-force password guessing, balanced against the risk of denial-of-service lockout abuse.

Orphaned account risk: accounts left active after role changes or departures are one of the most common findings in real penetration tests and compliance audits — they're low-visibility, high- impact residual risk.
troubleshooting: Symptom Likely Cause First Diagnostic Step User can't log in at all, correct password Account locked out, disabled, or expired Check account status in AD Users and Computers or `passwd -S username` on Linux User logs in but has none of their usual access Profile corruption, or account accidentally recreated with a new SID/UID instead of restored Compare the account's unique identifier (SID/UID) against backups or documentation, not just the username "Account locked" recurring repeatedly right after unlock A cached credential on a device (phone, mapped drive) is retrying an old password automatically Check Event Viewer for the source workstation/IP of failed logon attempts, not just the account New employee has access to things they shouldn't on day one Provisioned by cloning an existing employee's account/group membership instead of using a clean role template Review actual group memberships granted versus the intended role baseline Service stops working after a scheduled password rotation Service account's stored/cached credential wasn't updated everywhere it's used Check the service's configured logon account and any connection strings or scheduled task credentials Deleted user's files/mailbox inaccessible after account removal SID/UID was deleted before ownership was reassigned; deleting is often irreversible in a way disabling is not Always disable before deleting, and reassign file/mailbox ownership as part of the offboarding checklist
example: At a fintech-style operations company (comparable to a FundedNext support environment), a contractor is brought on for a three-month project and given a full domain user account cloned from a permanent employee's profile for convenience, rather than provisioned from a proper contractor role template. When the contract ends, HR notifies IT verbally, but no ticket is formally logged, and the account is simply forgotten.

Eight months later, a routine access audit for a compliance certification turns up the still-active, still- enabled account — with access to shared drives, an internal ticketing system, and a VPN profile — for someone who hasn't worked there in over half a year. Nothing malicious happened in this case, but the exposure window represents eight months where a former contractor (or anyone who obtained their credentials) could have accessed sensitive systems with no one watching.

The organization's fix directly mirrors the earlier permissions example: offboarding becomes a mandatory, ticket-tracked HR-to-IT handoff with same-day account disabling, contractor accounts get automatic expiration dates set at creation time rather than relying on someone remembering to remove them, and quarterly access reviews are instituted specifically to catch exactly this kind of drift before an external auditor does.
cloud: Cloud identity platforms (Azure AD/Entra ID, AWS IAM users, Google Cloud Identity) generalize the local user account concept to the entire cloud estate — a single cloud identity can control access across dozens of SaaS applications and cloud resources at once.

Federated identity increasingly means fewer standalone cloud accounts and more "log in with your corporate identity" flows (Session 63 — Federation, Session 64 — SSO), reducing the number of separate account lifecycles to manage.

Cloud environments distinguish human user identities from machine identities (service principals in Azure, IAM roles in AWS, service accounts in GCP) even more sharply than on-prem systems — machine identities in the cloud frequently outnumber human ones and require their own dedicated governance.

Just-in-time and Privileged Identity Management (Azure PIM, AWS IAM Identity Center permission sets) let organizations grant standing "eligible" access that only becomes "active" for a limited window, directly addressing the standing-privileged-account risk described in Section 8.
automation: Identity lifecycle automation (often called Joiner-Mover-Leaver, or JML) triggers account creation, group assignment, and deactivation automatically from an authoritative HR system feed rather than manual ticket handling.
PowerShell (New-ADUser, Disable-ADAccount, Get-ADUser -Filter) is the standard enterprise tool for bulk account operations and scripted audits of stale or expiring accounts.

Configuration management (Ansible's `user` module, Puppet's `user` resource type) keeps local Linux account existence, UID consistency, and shell/home directory settings enforced identically across large server fleets.

Automated access reviews: scheduled scripts or Identity Governance tooling (Session 66) that flag accounts with no login activity in N days, feeding directly into the offboarding/audit workflow described in Section 4.
career: User account administration is often a new IT professional's very first hands-on responsibility, and it remains a career-long thread through nearly every infrastructure and security role.
Help Desk / Support: password resets, account unlocks, and "why can't I log in" tickets are daily, high-volume work — directly the territory this roadmap is being built from.
Systems Administrator: designing and running the onboarding/offboarding pipeline, managing Active Directory user objects at scale.

Identity & Access Management (IAM) Specialist: an entire specialized career track focused exactly on this topic and its Layer 4 extensions — provisioning, governance, lifecycle automation, and access certification.
Security Analyst / Auditor: stale and over-privileged accounts are one of the most consistently cited findings in security assessments, making account hygiene a core audit skill.
Cloud/DevOps Engineer: managing human and machine identities across cloud platforms, and building the automation that keeps account lifecycles accurate without manual intervention.

For someone coming from a support role, deep fluency here — knowing exactly how account state, lockouts, and provisioning actually work under the hood rather than just clicking through a GUI — is a clear, visible differentiator when moving into a sysadmin or IAM-focused role.

misconceptions: "Deleting an account immediately is the safest response to an offboarding." — Deleting first (rather than disabling first) can orphan file ownership, break mailbox recovery, and destroy audit history;
best practice is disable now, delete later per retention policy.

"A username is the account's real identity." — The underlying UID/SID is the true identity the OS tracks; usernames are just a friendly label and can even be reused for a completely different SID later, which is exactly why renaming or reusing usernames requires care.

"Shared accounts save time and licensing cost with no real downside." — Shared accounts eliminate individual accountability entirely, which is treated as a serious control gap in virtually every security framework and audit standard.

"Service accounts don't need password rotation since no human types the password." — Service account credentials are exactly as valuable to an attacker as human credentials, often more so due to their broad access, and stale credentials are a major lateral-movement risk.

"A locked account and a disabled account are the same thing." — Locked usually means a temporary, self-resolving (or admin-resettable) state from failed login attempts; disabled is a deliberate, persistent administrative action — they require different fixes.

"Once someone's account is created correctly, it stays correct." — Access naturally drifts as people change roles and accumulate old group memberships ("permission creep"); accounts need periodic review, not just correct initial setup.
anchors: User account = employee badge; it proves identity to the system but doesn't itself open any doors — permissions and groups are the doors.
UID/SID = the badge's embedded chip, not the printed name on the front — the system trusts the chip, not the name.
Disable before delete = take the badge away and deactivate it, but keep it in the drawer in case HR or legal needs to ask questions about it later.
Service account = a badge issued to a robot, not a person — it never sleeps, never quits, and needs its own separate security policy.
Account lockout = three wrong door-code attempts and the keypad locks itself for a while — a defense against someone guessing all night.
Stale account = a badge still active for someone who moved out of the building months ago — invisible until someone actually checks the access log.
connections: Session 12 (Kernel): the kernel is what actually resolves a running process back to a UID/SID on every single permission check — user accounts are meaningless without the kernel's enforcement of that mapping.
Session 13 (Processes) & Session 14 (Threads): every process is launched under a specific user context, which directly determines what that process — and every thread within it — is allowed to touch.
Session 17 (Services): services are the clearest practical example of the human-account vs. service- account distinction introduced in this session.
Session 18 (Logging): security-relevant logs are only useful when log entries can be tied back to a specific, individually accountable user account rather than a shared or anonymous identity.

Session 19 (File Systems) & Session 20 (Permissions): file ownership (a user account) and the permission bits/ACLs attached to that ownership are two halves of the same access-control coin — this session supplies the "who" that Session 20's "what they can do" was built around.

This session sets up Groups (22) directly — the mechanism for managing many users' permissions at once — and is the essential prerequisite for the entire Layer 4 Identity block (Active Directory, Kerberos, SSO, MFA), since none of those systems mean anything without a well-understood concept of the user account they're authenticating and governing.

Diagrams (Described) Diagram A — Anatomy of a Linux user account [/etc/passwd entry: username:x:UID:GID:comment:home_dir:shell] → [/etc/shadow entry (separate, root- only): username:hashed_password:last_change:min:max:warn:inactive:expire] → [Group memberships defined in /etc/group]. The username is a lookup label; the UID is the number the kernel actually checks on every access.
Diagram B — Account lifecycle (Joiner-Mover-Leaver) [HR creates hire record] → [Joiner: IT provisions account from role template, assigns groups] → [Mover:

role/department changes, group memberships updated — old ones removed, not just new ones added] → [Leaver: HR notifies IT, account disabled same day] → [Retention period passes] → [Account deleted, data/ownership reassigned per policy].
Diagram C — Windows local vs. domain account resolution [User attempts logon] → [Is this a domain-joined machine and a domain-format credential?] → [Yes:

request forwarded to Domain Controller for authentication against Active Directory] → [No: checked against local SAM database on the machine itself] → [Success: token issued containing user SID + all group SIDs] → [Token used for every subsequent permission check during the session].
lab: Hands-on exercises to build real muscle memory. Use a disposable VM or test machine.
Linux 9. Create a new user with useradd -m -s /bin/bash testuser, set a password with passwd, and inspect the resulting entry in /etc/passwd.
10.Use chage -l testuser to view password aging settings, then set an explicit expiration date with chage -E.
11.Lock the account with usermod -L testuser, confirm login fails, then unlock it with usermod -U and confirm it works again.
12.Create a second account, then use id testuser and id seconduser to compare their UID/GID values directly rather than just usernames.
13.Disable (don't delete) testuser using usermod -L combined with an expired shell (usermod -s /usr/sbin/nologin), and explain why this is safer than deleting immediately.
Windows 14.Create a new local user via PowerShell (New-LocalUser), then view it in lusrmgr.msc to confirm it appears correctly.
15.Disable the account with Disable-LocalUser, attempt to log in, and confirm the specific error shown differs from a simple wrong-password error.
16.Use Get-LocalUser | Select Name, SID to view the actual SIDs behind your local accounts, and identify the well-known SID pattern for built-in Administrator.
